title: A belt of thunderstorms circles the Earth and follows the Sun north and south
body: Near the equator, the trade winds blowing from the north-east and the south-east meet, and where they converge, thunderstorms build into a band of cloud and rain that circles the planet. It is called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, and through the year it shifts north and south, **following the Sun** with a time lag, swinging farther from the equator over land than over the ocean. Its passing brings the tropics their wet and dry seasons. Over Asia the heavy rains [move between South Asia in the northern summer and Australia in the northern winter](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5254/), the seasonal shift of the [monsoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon_of_South_Asia).

slides.prompt: Eighteenth-century sailors had a name for this belt, because its winds were so often calm. What was it?
slides.detail: The name described its calm, stagnant winds. It was also called the calms.

events.text: The rains reach the coast of Kerala, near Thiruvananthapuram
The monsoon starts to withdraw, and is gone by early October

slides.label: of monsoon rain a year at both Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, in India
slides.text: That is more than 11,000 mm. The two places, in the state of Meghalaya, take turns holding the title of wettest place on Earth.

steps.label: In summer, land heats up faster than the sea
The pressure difference pulls sea air inland
The moist air drops heavy rain over the land

slides.question: In the clip, where does the heaviest rain fall in July and August?
slides.explanation: In the northern summer the rain belt and the Asian monsoon move north over South Asia; in the northern winter they shift south toward Australia.
